props.title: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit
props.initialSlug: The bunnies are back... and hungry!

sections.content: **Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit** (2005) represents Aardman Animation's crowning achievement in stop-motion clay animation. Building on the beloved short films like **A Grand Day Out** (1989) and **The Wrong Trousers** (1993), directors Nick Park and Steve Box crafted a feature-length adventure that maintains the quintessentially British charm while expanding the scope. The film's stunning attention to detail - from the expressive plasticine characters to the intricate vegetable-themed sight gags - required over 5 years of painstaking animation, with the team completing only 3 seconds of footage per day.

sections.content: The Were-Rabbit's horror-comedy fusion draws from classic Universal monster movies while maintaining family-friendly whimsy. Like **Young Frankenstein** (1974), it lovingly parodies genre tropes through the lens of comedy. The film's environmental themes and celebration of garden culture echo earlier Aardman works while adding sophisticated layers about conservation and community. The relationship between Wallace and Gromit continues the tradition of great silent comedy duos like Laurel & Hardy, with Gromit's expressiveness achieved purely through eyebrow movement. SUBHEAD: Stop-Motion Innovation and Influence

The technical achievements of Were-Rabbit pushed stop-motion boundaries, influencing later works like **ParaNorman** (2012) and **Kubo and the Two Strings** (2016). The film's success proved audiences would embrace feature-length stop-motion, paving the way for studios like Laika. The handcrafted aesthetic offers a striking alternative to computer animation, with every fingerprint and texture celebrating the artisanal nature of the medium. This tangible quality connects to earlier stop-motion pioneers like Ray Harryhausen and the works of Czech animator Jiří Trnka.
